lessons.title: Measurements and Units
lessons.objective: Apply SI units without hesitation: identify fundamental and derived units, measure regular and irregular bodies, read instruments to their least count, estimate errors, write standard form and check equations by dimensions.

content.heading: Measurements and Units
paragraphs: A painter quotes 2.1 metres on a wall; a grocer sells 1 kilogram of tomatoes. Every honest physics answer carries a number and a unit — no unit, no meaning.

content.heading: SI units, area and volume
paragraphs: SI has seven fundamental quantities and their units: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd). Everything else is derived from these.

Derived units come by multiplication and division: area m², volume m³, speed m/s; force = mass × acceleration = kg·m/s² = newton (N); energy = kg·m²/s² = joule (J); power = J/s = watt (W). Regular bodies use formulas: square a², rectangle lw, circle πr², cube a³, cuboid lwh, cylinder πr²h, sphere ⁴⁄₃πr³.
Prefixes: 1 km = 10³ m, 1 cm = 10⁻² m, 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m.
bullets: Fundamentals: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd
Derived: m², m³, m/s, N, J, W
Regular: square a², circle πr², cuboid lwh, cylinder πr²h
content.takeaway: A unit is an identity card — carry it through every line of the calculation.

check.question: Which of these is an SI derived unit?
check.why: The newton combines fundamental units (kg·m/s²); the ampere and the kelvin are fundamental, and the kilometre is a prefixed metre.

content.heading: Measuring instruments and their least counts
paragraphs: Instruments match their job: metre rule ±1 mm; vernier caliper ±0.1 mm (measures tubes inside); micrometer screw gauge ±0.01 mm; measuring cylinder — irregular solid volume by displacement; stop watch 0.01–0.1 s; beam balance (Buchert’s/chemical) matches unknown masses.

Least count is the smallest interval on the scale; the best reading any instrument gives is true ± half its least count. Accuracy is how near the truth a reading lies; precision is how finely it reads.

Common errors: parallax (view from above — the object appears shifted), zero error (reads non-zero at zero — subtract for positive, add for negative), calibration (marks misplaced). Estimate simple error as ± half a least count.
bullets: metre rule ±1 mm; vernier ±0.1 mm; micrometer ±0.01 mm
Irregular solids: displacement method with a measuring cylinder
Simple error estimate: half a least count; fix zero error first
content.takeaway: Match the instrument to the size — a ruler cannot do a micrometer's job.

check.question: The least count of a micrometer screw gauge is
check.why: Each thimble division advances the spindle by 0.01 mm, which is the least count of a standard micrometer.

content.heading: Dimensions, homogeneity and standard form
paragraphs: Every derived unit has a dimension in M, L and T. Speed LT⁻¹; acceleration LT⁻²; force MLT⁻²; energy ML²T⁻²; pressure ML⁻¹T⁻²; power ML²T⁻³.

Get dimensions from definitions: force = mass × acceleration = MLT⁻². Use them to (1) deduce forgotten units — replace unit letters with dimensions and compare powers; (2) test homogeneity — both sides must carry identical powers of M, L and T.

Standard form: exactly one digit left of the point — 46,200 = 4.62 × 10⁴; 0.000321 = 3.21 × 10⁻⁴. Significant figures: non-zero digits count; zeros between non-zero digits count; leading zeros do not; closing zeros in a decimal do.
bullets: M, L and T alone — never kg or seconds
Both sides of an equation must match: v² = u² + 2as → each side L²T⁻²
content.takeaway: An equation can be dimensionally correct and numerically wrong — dimensions check possibility, not truth.

check.question: The dimension of power is
check.why: Power = work ÷ time = (ML²T⁻²) ÷ T = ML²T⁻³.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB derives units and homogeneity most years. Replace unit letters with dimensions, compare powers on each side, and impossible formulas collapse on sight.

content.problem: Check whether v² = u² + 2as is dimensionally homogeneous.

steps.reason: v, u velocities (LT⁻¹); a acceleration (LT⁻²); s displacement (L)
steps.predictPrompt: What powers of L and T hide inside v²? Work them out before looking.

steps.reason: only terms with identical dimensions can be added
steps.predictPrompt: Can you add terms whose powers differ?

steps.reason: homogeneity is necessary for any equation to be possible
steps.result: Both sides are L²T⁻² — the equation is homogeneous
steps.predictPrompt: What would mismatched powers tell you?

content.question: Use dimensions to show that the newton (N) is equivalent to kg·m/s².
hints: Dimension is MLT⁻² — collect the powers of M, L and T.
So a newton must carry one  M, one  L and T to the power −2; that is kg·m/s².

content.heading: A harder worked example: find a missing unit with dimensions
content.problem: Use the equation PV = nRT to find the unit of the gas constant R. P is pressure (N/m²), V is volume (m³), n in moles, T in kelvin.

steps.reason: pressure = N/m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻²; volume m³ — P × V removes one m
steps.predictPrompt: What powers of m survive when you multiply kg·m⁻¹·s⁻² by m³?

steps.result: R has the unit kg·m²·s⁻²·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹ — identical to J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹
steps.predictPrompt: Which IS-unit does that product equal?

content.heading: Go deeper: reading a vernier caliper and a micrometer
paragraphs: A vernier caliper refines one main-scale millimetre into ten equal vernier divisions, so each vernier division is 0.1 mm. Its reading is MSR (main scale reading just before the vernier zero) + the division on the vernier scale that coincides with a main-scale mark × 0.1 mm. Example: MSR = 2.4 cm and the 7th vernier division coincides — length = 2.4 + 0.07 = 2.47 cm.

A micrometer screw gauge goes smaller: each sleeve mark is 0.5 mm (half a millimetre), and the thimble is divided into 50, so each thimble division advances the spindle by 0.01 mm. Its reading is sleeve reading + thimble division coinciding × 0.01 mm. Example: sleeve reads 6.5 mm and the 27th thimble division aligns with the sleeve line — length = 6.5 + 0.27 = 6.77 mm.

Both instruments have an optional depth rod or outside jaws (vernier) and an anvil/spindle (micrometer). Strings and dividers measure non-straight objects: wind a string along the curve, mark its ends, then measure the straight string against a ruler. A zero error is corrected BEFORE adding anything: if the micrometer reads +0.02 mm at zero, subtract 0.02 mm from every reading.
bullets: Vernier: MSR + (coinciding vernier division) × 0.1 mm
Micrometer: sleeve + (coinciding thimble division) × 0.01 mm
No device can beat its least count — estimate ± half a division
content.takeaway: Add the main scale and the vernier/thimble reading — then fix the zero error.

content.heading: Go deeper: errors, accuracy and significant figures
paragraphs: Errors come in two families. Systematic errors push every reading the same way — a mismarked scale, a zero error, parallax viewed from above (the object appears shifted toward the eye). Random errors scatter readings either way and cancel over many tries. JAMB consistently asks the difference, and 'calibrate before you measure' is the exam's expected fix.

Accuracy is how near the truth a reading lies; precision is how repeatable or fine it is. A leaky beam balance is precise (same wrong reading every time) but inaccurate (never sees the truth). Percentage error is |(experimental − accepted) ÷ accepted| × 100% — a lab favourite; simple estimate error is half the least count.

Significant figures follow three rules: non-zero digits are always significant; zeros between non-zero digits are significant (205 has three); leading zeros never are (0.0024 has two: 2 and 4); closing zeros after a decimal point are (4.50 has three). In standard form every digit shown is significant — 4.50 × 10³ signals three figures, while 4.5 × 10³ signals two.
bullets: Systematic: same-way push; random: scatters then cancels
Percent error = (exp − acc) ÷ acc × 100%
4.50 × 10³ ≠ 4.5 × 10³ — closing zeros signal precision
content.takeaway: Quote as many figures as the instrument actually delivers.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets questions on this topic
paragraphs: The IBASS syllabus lists this topic as the entry point to physics — and JAMB's question bank reflects it. Internally this topic carries one of the biggest single-topic totals in the 1983–2004 archive (27 mapped items). The recurring archetypes are: (1) 'which of these is a fundamental unit?' — the safe order is m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd; (2) 'deduce the unit of X' with dimensions; (3) 'which equation is homogeneous?' — or which term fits the gap; (4) standard form conversion, either direction; (5) significant figures counting.

Instrument variation: metre rule vs vernier vs micrometer — the silt test is 'how precisely does this measure a diameter?' Answer: micrometer > vernier > metre rule. An irregular stone in an overflow can collects a measured volume of water — that is the stone's volume (top up the can to the brim first). A stop watch never measures anything well to 0.1 s below; small falls need light gates.

Compound variations fold two operations into one stem: 'a vernier reads 2.47 cm — write it in standard form and express its percentage error vs an accepted 2.50 cm.' Answer in two steps: 2.47 × 10⁻² m; error = |2.47 − 2.50| / 2.50 × 100 = 1.2%. Practise both moves until the sequence is automatic — most candidates drop the mark on the percent step, not the subtraction.
bullets: Fundamental vs derived pick-the-odd-one-out
Homogeneity: term missing from u² + 2as — try LT counterweights
Overflow can value = volume of the solid placed in it
content.takeaway: The archive shows the recurring variation list — drill the eight, not the hundred.

lessons.title: Scalars and Vectors
lessons.objective: Distinguish scalars from vectors, resolve and combine vectors by the parallelogram law, find components and solve relative-velocity problems for river crossings, rain and travelling bodies.

content.heading: Scalars and Vectors
paragraphs: 5 metres, or 5 metres north — the number is the same; the direction changes everything. Physics values both.

content.heading: Scalars versus vectors
paragraphs: A scalar has magnitude only: mass, length, area, volume, time, speed, energy, work, temperature, density, pressure, distance. A vector has magnitude and direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, weight, thrust, moment of a couple.

The one-line test: does a change in direction change the answer? If not, it is a scalar (60 km is 60 km whichever way it goes); if yes, it is a vector. Distance is the path walked; displacement is the straight line from start to finish with direction. Velocity is a vector; speed is not.
bullets: Scalars: m, kg, s, time, distance, speed, energy, work, temperature, pressure
Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum, weight
watch the speed–velocity trap
content.takeaway: Add arrows on vectors only — adding arrows to scalars changes nothing.

check.question: Which list contains only scalar quantities?
check.why: Only mass, distance and area are direction-free; the others contain at least one vector.

content.heading: Resultant of two or more vectors
paragraphs: Same line: vectors add algebraically. 20 N east + 12 N east = 32 N east; opposite lines subtract. At right angles, use Pythagoras — e.g. a force of 3 N east and 4 N north give R = √(3² + 4²) = 5 N.
Any angle θ: R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQcosθ). For equal forces P: R = 2Pcos(θ/2). cosθ goes negative beyond 90° — for obtuse angles R shrinks below √(P² + Q²).
Resolution reverses it: F splits into Fcosθ (along) and Fsinθ (across). A 20 N force at 30° to the horizontal → 17.3 N along, 10 N up — the move JAMB uses on inclined planes.
bullets: Same line: add; right angle: R = √(P² + Q²)
Any angle: R = √(P² + Q² + 2PQcosθ)
Components: Fcosθ (along), Fsinθ (across)
content.takeaway: Draw a rough sketch first — vectors are safer on paper than in memory.

check.question: Forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles to each other. Their resultant is
check.why: Perpendicular forces: R = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5 N. Direction θ = tan⁻¹(4/3) = 53°.

content.heading: Relative velocity
paragraphs: Relative velocity = your velocity minus mine on the same frame. Same direction: u − v; opposite direction: u + v. Two cars meeting at 25 m/s and 15 m/s pass at 40 m/s.
Crossing motion (frames perpendicular): a swimmer at 4 m/s faces a river flowing at 3 m/s — R = √(4² + 3²) = 5 m/s, crossing time = width ÷ 4 m/s regardless of current, drift = 3 m/s × time.
Rain and running-man: apparent slant tanθ = run ÷ rain; apparent speed = √(rain² + run²). Rain at 12 m/s on a man running at 5 m/s → slant ≈ 23°, apparent speed 13 m/s.
bullets: Same line: u − v same direction; u + v opposite
Across a river: R = √(u² + v²); drift = v × crossing time
Rain: tanθ = speed of runner ÷ speed of rain
content.takeaway: Relative velocity is vector addition — draw two arrows and close the triangle.

check.question: A swimmer swims at 4 m/s across a river flowing at 3 m/s. The resultant speed is
check.why: Frames are perpendicular: R = √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5 m/s.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB's vector trap: two forces of equal size do not automatically add up. Unless it says 'same direction' or 'at right angles', reach for the parallelogram formula or a scale diagram.

content.problem: Two forces 5 N and 7 N act at 60° to each other. Find the magnitude of their resultant.

steps.reason: R² = P² + Q² + 2PQcosθ; P = 5 N, Q = 7 N, θ = 60°
steps.predictPrompt: cos60° without a calculator — what is it?
What number replaces 70 × 0.5?

steps.reason: take the positive square root — force is a magnitude
steps.predictPrompt: If θ were 120°, would R be bigger or smaller?

content.question: Resolve a 20 N force acting at 30° to the horizontal into its horizontal and vertical components.

content.heading: A harder worked example: the river-crossing triplet
content.problem: A swimmer swims at 4 m/s in still water. A river is 50 m wide and flows at 3 m/s. Find (a) the angle upstream to land directly opposite, (b) the crossing time, (c) the resultant speed.

steps.reason: the swimmer's upstream component must cancel the current: sinθ = current ÷ own speed
steps.predictPrompt: If the current were faster than his swimming speed, could he ever land opposite?

steps.reason: crossing uses his own speed across the river, not the resultant
steps.predictPrompt: Why does the current not enter this calculation?

steps.reason: velocity is the vector sum of his speed and the current
steps.predictPrompt: What would (c) be if he ignored the current and swam straight across?

content.heading: Go deeper: the parallelogram law, step by step
paragraphs: Two forces acting on a body can be replaced by a single force. Draw one force from O: e.g. 5 N along the line OX. Draw the second force from the same O at the given angle: e.g. 7 N along the line OA. These two arrows are two sides of a parallelogram; complete the opposite two sides by drawing parallellines; the diagonal from O is the resultant.

Measure the diagonal with a ruler against your chosen scale (e.g. 1 cm = 1 N) and measure its angle with a protractor from OX. Expect some small measurement error — JAMB allows a window (e.g. R between 10 N and 11 N) in graphical questions.

Analytical alternative for the same wheelhouse: R² = P² + Q² + 2PQcosθ (for an angle θ between P and Q). If θ = 180°, R = |P − Q| — the vectors cancel. If θ = 0°, R = P + Q — pure addition. Obtuse angles shrink R; do not be surprised to get R smaller than either force.
bullets: Draw OX for P and OA for Q; parallel sides complete the figure
Measure the diagonal with the scale you started with
cosθ is negative for obtuse angles — the law still works
content.takeaway: Paper first: a quick sketch decides which formula applies.

content.heading: Go deeper: resolving vectors into perpendicular parts
paragraphs: Any vector can be split into two perpendicular components. For the vector F at angle θ from the horizontal, the horizontal (adjacent) component is Fcosθ and the vertical (opposite) component is Fsinθ. This is why a 20 N pull at 30° to the ground moves a crate with 17.3 N horizontal force and 10 N lifting vertically.

The reverse: from components you can rebuild the vector — F = √(Fₓ² + F_y²), tanθ = F_y/Fₓ. In two dimensions this is exactly the Cartesian resynthesis from vectors (x, y) to their length, and it mirrors the x-y plane you use in displacement questions.

JAMB loves components on an inclined plane: a block of weight W on a slope at angle θ experiences Wcosθ into the slope and Wsinθ along the slope downward. The friction needed to keep it still is therefore f = μWcosθ, and to keep it from sliding, the applied force along the plane must equal Wsinθ − f.
bullets: Horizontal (adjacent): Fcosθ
Vertical (opposite): Fsinθ; rebuild: √(Fₓ² + F_y), tanθ = F_y/Fₓ
Incline: Wparallel = Wsinθ; Wperpendicular = Wcosθ
content.takeaway: Resolution is not a trick — it is how physics splits problems into convenient directions.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets relative-velocity questions
paragraphs: Relative motion is a favourite because it hides a simple idea inside a busy story. The archive maps 23 items against this topic. The archetypes: (1) same-line opposite pass — add the two speeds, e.g. two trains approaching, relative velocity is their sum; (2) same direction — subtract, e.g. the faster overtaking the slower; (3) perpendicular crossing — boats, swimmers and river currents; use R = √(u² + v²).

Time-related variations ask for (a) crossing time = width ÷ own swim speed; (b) drift distance = current speed × crossing time; (c) landing angle = tan⁻¹(drift ÷ width). Rain and running man: apparent slant θ = tan⁻¹(run speed ÷ rain speed) and apparent velocity √(rain² + run²). Both questions expect a scale sketch or a tan⁻¹ press after substitution.

One trap JAMB sets repeatedly: 'a boat crosses a 40 m river in 10 s; the current is 3 m/s; find the boat's own swimming speed.' The crossing time uses own speed — divide 40 by 10 to get 4 m/s, then R = √(4² + 3²) = 5 m/s resultant. The reverse trap: 'find the actual speed of the boat' invites √(3² + 4²) while the 'crossing component' is simply 40/10 = 4 m/s.
bullets: Same direction: subtract; opposite: add
River: t = width ÷ own speed; drift = current × t
Rain: tanθ = run speed ÷ rain speed
content.takeaway: Boats, rain and trains are the same question wearing three hats.

lessons.title: Measurement, position, distance and displacement
lessons.objective: Measure length and angles with accurate instruments, locate positions on Cartesian and compass-bearing grids, distinguish distance from displacement, and read or infer from kinematic graphs.

content.heading: Measurement, position, distance and displacement
paragraphs: A driver from Kano to Kaduna travels 200 km of road; the towns are barely 175 km apart in a straight line. Both figures are true — distance walks, displacement cuts. Physics needs both.

content.heading: Measuring lengths with least counts
paragraphs: Instruments match their job: metre rule ±1 mm; vernier caliper ±0.1 mm (inner/outer jaws, depth rod); micrometer screw gauge ±0.01 mm; measuring cylinder millilitres; stopwatch 0.01–0.1 s; beam balance (Buchert’s/chemical) matches masses.

Accuracy is how near the truth; precision is how fine. Both fall to zero error — the instrument reads non-zero at zero. Correct before calculating: add for negative zero error, subtract for positive. Estimate simple error as ± half a least count.

Strings and dividers measure curves: wind a string along the bend, mark the ends, read the straight string on a ruler. A compass and a protractor lay off and read bearings — angles clockwise from north, 0°–360°.
bullets: metre rule ±1 mm; vernier ±0.1 mm; micrometer ±0.01 mm
Simple error estimate: ± half a least count
Compass + protractor: bearings 0°–360° clockwise from north
content.takeaway: Match instrument size to object size — a ruler never does a micrometer's job.

check.question: The least count of a vernier caliper is
check.why: The vernier subdivides one millimetre of main scale into ten parts, so each vernier division is 0.1 mm.

content.heading: Position, distance and displacement
paragraphs: Position is a point in space from a fixed reference (origin). On Cartesian (x, y) coordinates, x is measured east and y north; (6, 8) is 6 east, 8 north of (0, 0).
Distance is total path — a scalar: 3 km east plus 4 km north is 7 km. Displacement is the straight line start→finish with direction — a vector: √(3² + 4²) = 5 km, tanθ = 4/3, θ ≈ 53° north of east.
Frame of reference fixes motion. In a moving train, your friend beside you barely moves; from the rails you both do. Physics always names its observer.
bullets: Position: a point measured from (0, 0), e.g. (2, 3)
Distance = 7 km (scalar) vs displacement = 5 km at 53° (vector)
Always state the frame — train/ground/car/ship
content.takeaway: Distance is the walk; displacement is the arrow from start to finish.

check.question: A body moves from (2, 3) to (6, 6) on a grid. Its displacement magnitude is
check.why: The coordinate difference is (4, 3), so displacement = √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5 units.

content.heading: Graphs of motion and their inference
paragraphs: Distance–time graph: gradient = speed, steeper line = faster. Displacement–time graph: gradient = velocity (negative = returning). Velocity–time graph: gradient = acceleration, area under it = distance travelled.
Constant velocity → flat line; acceleration → straight line, gradient ≠ 0; deceleration → sloping down. Area: triangle ½bh, rectangle bh, trapezium ½(a + b)h.

Reading a drawn graph: intercept (value at x = 0); gradient from two far-apart points ((y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁)); area below the curve. JAMB wants: (i) gradient or area, (ii) labelled axes, (iii) best-fit line, (iv) where two curves cross — when two bodies meet.
bullets: gradient of distance–time = speed; of displacement–time = velocity
gradient of velocity–time = acceleration
area under velocity–time = distance
content.takeaway: Every graph is a formula waiting to be read — gradient tells one law, area tells another.

check.question: On a velocity–time graph, the gradient gives the
check.why: Gradient = change in velocity ÷ time elapsed = acceleration.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Motion: the most-mapped archive topic (71 items). The split: scalar vs vector, read the gradient, find the area — three moves.

content.problem: A man walks 3 km east then 4 km north. Find (a) distance travelled, (b) displacement (magnitude and direction).

steps.predictPrompt: Would you still get 7 km if he walked 4 km north before the 3 km east?

steps.reason: start & finish join by the shortest line; legs are perpendicular
steps.predictPrompt: Before you open roots: is 3-4-5 triangle or not?
Would a calculator give θ ≈ 53.13°? Why is the exam-writer's expected answer 53°?

content.question: From a velocity–time graph, a car accelerates uniformly from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. Find (i) its acceleration; (ii) the distance covered in those 5 s.
hints: Gradient = Δv ÷ Δt; area under v–t graph = distance
Distance = area of triangle = ½ × 5 × 20 = 50 m

content.heading: A harder worked example: triangular and rectangular areas on one graph
content.problem: A bus accelerates uniformly from 6 m/s to 18 m/s in 4 s, then travels at constant speed for 6 s. Find (a) the distance covered in the first 4 s, (b) the distance covered in the next 6 s, (c) the average speed for the whole journey.

steps.reason: graph starts at 6 m/s, ends at 18 m/s — trapezium
steps.predictPrompt: Is the shape a triangle, a rectangle or a trapezium? Look at the start and end points.
What is the gradient in this part? Does it matter for the area?
If you instead averaged just the speeds, 12 and 18 — the answer would still differ. Which is correct?

content.heading: Go deeper: vernier and micrometer practice
paragraphs: A worked vernier reading: main scale 2.4 cm, the 7th vernier mark aligns — length = 2.47 cm. That is honest precision to 1 hundredth of a centimetre, ±0.0005 cm by half a least count. A worked micrometer reading: sleeve 6.5 mm visible, thimble mark 27 on the reference line — length = 6.5 + 0.27 = 6.77 mm, ±0.005 mm.

Zero error can creep either way. Vernier placed so its zeros do not coincide, with the vernier zero left of main zero: error is positive — subtract |the reading|. If the reading at zero is 0.06 mm, every measurement is 0.06 mm too high; subtract it. Micrometer zero behaves the same; always zero-check before you trust a result.

Composite reading: add MSR and the vernier part, then apply the zero correction last — never in the middle. JAMB's signature stem: 'A measurement reads 3.26 cm; the vernier actually reads 0 after zero check; express the error relative to an accepted 3.20 cm.' Answer in two steps: absolute error = 0.06 cm; percentage error = 0.06 ÷ 3.20 × 100 = 1.875%.
bullets: MSR + vernier part − zero correction
Never chain the zero correction into the vernier count
Percentage error = |exp − acc| ÷ acc × 100%
content.takeaway: Zero-check first, then add, then correct.

content.heading: Go deeper: bearings, compass and protractor
paragraphs: A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north, running 0° (north) through 90° (east), 180° (south) and 270° (west) back to 360°. Vector directions in physics are often stated as bearings — 'N 53° E' or 'bearing 053°' both mean the same direction, 53° east of north.

Reduced bearings shorten it further — e.g. N 40° E is bearing 040°, S 25° W is bearing 205°. A compass sets the plane: map north lies toward page top; a clockwise protractor reads bearings sweeping from that line.

JAMB uses this for riverbanks, ship lanes and runways. A question may give a sketch to scale — 'A boat leaves A and heads N 60° E for 100 m. B is the destination. Find its scale displacement.' Convert to x–y: east component = 100sin60° = 86.6 m; north = 100cos60° = 50 m. The bearing structure rides unchanged into vector addition.
bullets: Bearings clockwise from north: 0–360°
N 53° E = bearing 053°; S 25° W = bearing 205°
Split by bearing: N = Rcosθ, E = Rsinθ for N x E phrasing
content.takeaway: Draw the compass rose on paper first — bearings never confuse the drawn page.

content.heading: Go deeper: archetypes in kinematic graphs
paragraphs: The archive puts motion among the most-tested physics topics (71 mapped items). Graph variations concentrate into four: (1) read gradient — speed or acceleration between two drawn points; (2) find area — distance travelled between two times (usually a triangle, rectangle or trapezium); (3) draw the best-fit line and infer proportionality — distance ∝ time signals constant speed; (4) two bodies on one graph — 'when do they meet?' = read the x where the two curves intersect.

Compound archetype: a table with times and distances, plot and compute speed. Trend lines straight ⇒ speed = gradient = Δy ÷ Δx. Where non-linearity appears, acceleration is changing, and the graph turns up or down from a parabola-like curve; the gradient at one instant is the tangent slope, not the secant.

Trap variations to expect: the axes deliberately swap ('time along y, distance along x' — gradient then gives seconds per metre, the reciprocal of speed — reverse the labels before calculating); the shaded band is 'uncertainty' to be added as a result range; a second graph includes deceleration — remember area still wins: every square centimetre below the curve counts, up to the last axis point.
bullets: gradient = speed (d–t graph) or acceleration (v–t graph)
area under v–t = distance; intercept = initial value
Two curves meet → that is the time of meeting
content.takeaway: Graphs in physics are arithmetic wearing a diagram's clothes.

lessons.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
lessons.objective: Identify types of motion, push/pull and contact/field forces, inertia, mass and weight, and apply Newton's three laws to worked problems; compare mass and weight; read force as the cause of motion.

content.heading: Forces and Newton's Laws
paragraphs: A lorry stalls at a zebra crossing and two boys push. Why does the lorry move only now — and why does it hurt less when they push gently? Newton's laws turn that everyday argument into three questions every physics question secretly asks.

content.heading: Types of motion and force
paragraphs: Motion comes in five shapes: translational (straight-line movement of a car or train), rotational (a spinning wheel), vibrational or oscillatory (a pendulum, a tuning fork), spin (a top, the Earth itself) and random (the zigzag of gas molecules — Brownian motion).

Force is that which changes a body's state of rest or motion, or its shape — a push or a pull. Contact forces act at touching points: friction, tension, normal reaction, air resistance. Field forces act at a distance: gravity, magnetic force, electric force.
bullets: Translational → straight-line; rotational → turning; vibrational → back-and-forth
Contact: friction, tension, reaction, drag
Field: gravity, magnetism, electric force — act across empty space
content.takeaway: Force is the cause; the body's change is the effect — never the other way round.

check.question: Which of the following is NOT a contact force?
check.why: Magnetic force is a field force — it acts across empty space with no contact.

content.heading: Inertia, mass and Newton's first law
paragraphs: Inertia is a body's tendency to resist changes in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line. More mass, more inertia. Newton's first law: a body at rest stays at rest, and a body in motion moves at constant velocity, until a resultant external force acts on it.

Mass is the measure of inertia — a scalar, in kilograms, constant everywhere. Weight is the gravitational pull on that mass — a vector, W = mg, and it changes with g: a 60 kg person registers 600 N on Earth and about 100 N on the Moon.
bullets: 1st law: resisting change — both at rest and in motion
Mass (kg) = how much; weight (N) = pull caused by gravity
g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth; Moon weight ≈ Earth weight ÷ 6
content.takeaway: Heavier means harder to move, stop, swerve — that is inertia in one line.

check.question: A moving stone keeps moving forward mainly because of its
check.why: Newton's first law: the stone continues in straight-line motion until an external force stops it.

content.heading: Newton's second and third laws
paragraphs: Newton's second law: the acceleration of a body is proportional to the resultant force on it, in the direction of that force, and inversely proportional to its mass — F = ma. Double the force, double the acceleration; double the mass, halve it.
The same law in momentum form is F = (mv − mu) ÷ t — the net force equals the rate of change of momentum. That is impulse; the next lesson builds on it.

Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. A swimmer pushes water backward; the water pushes the swimmer forward. A rocket expels gas downward; the gas lifts the rocket.
bullets: F = ma — force in newtons, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s²
Two overriding questions: size of F and direction of F
3rd law pairs always act on two different bodies
content.takeaway: F = ma is the single most-used equation in the paper — name the mass first, then the net force.

check.question: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 2 m/s². The resultant force on it is
check.why: F = ma = 1200 × 2 = 2400 N, in the direction of the acceleration.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Almost every force question reduces to F = ma or W = mg. First find the mass, then the net force; direction carries the sign of a 2D problem.

content.problem: A 5 kg trolley is pushed by a resultant force of 15 N on a frictionless surface. Find (a) its acceleration, (b) its velocity after 4 s, starting from rest.

steps.predictPrompt: Which quantity do you divide by mass here — force or weight?
Does the acceleration change during the 4 s?

content.question: A 2 kg mass at rest is pushed by a 10 N force for 3 s. Find its acceleration and its velocity after 3 s.
hints: v = u + at with u = 0 → v = 5 × 3 = 15 m/s
p = mv = 2 × 15 = 30 kg·m/s — useful for the next lesson

content.heading: A harder worked example: two forces, one motion
content.problem: Forces 30 N due east and 40 N due north act simultaneously on a 10 kg body. Find (a) the resultant force, (b) the acceleration of the body.

steps.predictPrompt: Are these forces perpendicular? Check before reaching for Pythagoras.

steps.result: a = 50 ÷ 10 = 5 m/s² in the direction of R
steps.predictPrompt: In which direction is 'the direction of R' — north of east or east of north?

content.heading: Go deeper: Newton in everyday stories
paragraphs: Book stops suddenly. When a bus brakes hard, everything inside continues forward — you lurch, and passengers who stood without holding a rail may fall forward over seats. That is inertia refusing to drop from motion to rest with the bus. A seatbelt quietly supplies the external force that forces you to stop with the vehicle.

Starting the bus reverses the effect — the body stays behind while the bus moves forward; a passenger falls backward without a handhold. The unseen actor in both cases is not friction inside the bus but inertia outside your hand's reach.

Rowing and swimming run on the third law: you push water backward; it pushes you forward. A rocket works the same way — the engine expels gas at high speed downward, and the gas pushes the rocket upward. Everyday rockets follow the same rule; launches work in space because the gas itself is the reaction mass — no ground to push against.
bullets: Sudden stop → lurch forward; sudden start → lurch backward
Rocket launch: gas down, rocket up — no launch pad needed
Third-law pair: two bodies, two forces, equal and opposite
content.takeaway: Read the story; identify inertia, mass, contact force or field force.

content.heading: Go deeper: mass, weight and g on different worlds
paragraphs: Mass is amount of matter — its SI unit is the kilogram, measured by comparison on a beam balance, and it is the same everywhere: a 60 kg crate weighs 60 kg on a spring balance marked in kg-force on Earth or the Moon. Weight is the force with which gravity pulls that mass — newtons, measured by a spring balance. On Earth, g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (physics problems often round to 10). On the Moon, g ≈ 1.6 m/s², so the same crate registers about one-sixth of its Earth weight — one-seventh when quoted in kg-force, one-sixth in newtons; JAMB expects one-sixth.

Weight acts through the centre of gravity; for a uniform object it is the geometric centre. A spring balance stretches more in a faster-rising lift in free fall — apparent weight changes, true weight does not.

g falls from the equator toward the poles (equatorial bulge — Earth is wider there, so distance from the centre grows and g shrinks) and falls with altitude. A small variation JAMB asks sometimes: mass stays put; weight does not travel well.
bullets: Mass: scalar, kg, anywhere. Weight: vector, N, varies with g
Moon: g ≈ 1.6 m/s² ≈ Earth weight ÷ 6
Beam balance compares masses; spring balance measures weight
content.takeaway: Mass is what you are made of; weight is how hard the planet pulls you.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets questions on this topic
paragraphs: The archetypes fall into four piles. (1) 'A resultant force of X acts on mass Y — find acceleration': pure F = ma. (2) Field vs contact identification: 'Which is NOT a contact force' — answers are always field forces. (3) Inertia puzzles: a coin on a card above a glass — flick the card and the coin falls into the glass — inertia, nothing else. (4) Impulse bridges: 'a force of 5 N for 2 s' asks you to either use F = ma or Ft = Δp — both lead to the same answer; JAMB accepts the line you choose.

Force-field confusion shows up as 'an object falls because of —': gravity. 'A soap bubble rises because of —': upthrust is not on the list; the answer is buoyancy only when the stem names a fluid. 'A magnet attracts the iron filings' — field. 'A crane lifts a load' — tension, a contact force delivered through the cable.

The net-force trap: 'the net force on the bus is zero, so it is stationary' — wrong; the bus can move at constant velocity. In football and car crashes, safety belts and airbags extend the stopping time, which reduces the average force for the same momentum change — directly off Ft = Δp.
bullets: F = ma or Ft = Δp — pick whichever numbers the question gives
Field force = no contact needed; contact = touching the body
Airbags and cushions: longer t, smaller F — same Δp
content.takeaway: JAMB asks the same force story in four costumes — learn the costumes.

lessons.title: Impulse and Momentum
lessons.objective: Apply momentum (p = mv), impulse (FΔt = Δp), force–time graphs and the law of conservation of linear momentum to collisions and explosions; distinguish momentum from kinetic energy.

content.heading: Impulse and Momentum
paragraphs: A barefoot kick hurts; the same kick with a football boot hardly registers. The force is identical; the contact time is not, and that is momentum — the quantity that cares how hard and for how long something pushes.

content.heading: Momentum and impulse
paragraphs: Momentum p = mv; unit kg·m/s. A 1500 kg car at 20 m/s carries 30,000 kg·m/s; a 0.05 kg ball at 30 m/s carries 1.5.
Impulse is force × time: I = FΔt = Δp = mv − mu; unit N·s, same as kg·m/s. A longer or harder push delivers more impulse.
F = ma and FΔt = Δp are the same law seen two ways. The Δt version handles any force profile — constant, falling or spiked; ma only handles a constant net force.
bullets: p = mv — scalar or vector? A vector, same direction as velocity
Impulse I = FΔt = Δp — unit N·s, same unit as momentum
Area depth: the area under a force–time graph = impulse
content.takeaway: Momentum is how much oomph a body carries; impulse is how quickly it gets there.

check.question: A 0.4 kg bat hits a stationary ball and gives it a velocity of 20 m/s. The impulse is

content.heading: Force–time graphs
paragraphs: Plot force on the y-axis and time on the x-axis and the shaded area between the curve and the time axis equals the impulse delivered — which equals the momentum change.
For simple shapes: a rectangle gives F × t; a triangle gives ½ × base × height — e.g., a 4 s burst peaking at 10 N delivers ½ × 4 × 10 = 20 N·s of impulse (20 kg·m/s of momentum, from rest).
For a trapezium, area = ½ (a + b) × height. JAMB reads them both ways: 'estimate the impulse from the graph' (compute the area) and 'the force–time graph shows … find the momentum change'.
bullets: Rectangle: F × t. Triangle: ½ × b × h. Trapezium: ½(a+b)h
Negative impulse? Check whether the force dips below the axis
Area under F–t graph ⇔ momentum change
content.takeaway: Area is the legal shorthand — mark the y-intercept, then sweep left to right.

check.question: A force–time graph shows a triangle with base 4 s and peak 10 N. The momentum gained by a body starting from rest is
check.why: Impulse = area = ½ × 4 × 10 = 20 kg·m/s; by FΔt = Δp, the body gains 20 kg·m/s of momentum.

content.heading: Conservation of momentum
paragraphs: When no external force acts, total momentum is conserved: p_before = p_after. For two bodies, m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂, along any one axis.

Uses: cannon recoil (cannon backward, shell forward — total momentum still zero), explosion separation (two pieces fly apart — total stays zero), a car picking up a passenger (the shove is internal; total is unchanged), and inelastic collisions where the two bodies stick together.

Kinetic energy is not conserved in most collisions — the lost energy becomes heat, sound and deformation. Momentum alone tracks. Coefficient of restitution is not needed for JAMB; the diagram + 'stuck together' is the standard stem.
bullets: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ — always along one axis
Sticky collisions: final masses merge, single v
Explosion: start from rest → two pieces fly apart, total p = 0
content.takeaway: Sum of momentum before = sum after — the only conservation JAMB needs on forces.

check.question: A 1000 kg car moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2000 kg car and they move together. Their common velocity is

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB never asks for restitution. Almost every collision stem is one line of momentum: sum before = sum after — draw the trolley diagram first.

content.problem: A 0.05 kg ball strikes a wall at 30 m/s and rebounds at 30 m/s. Find the impulse.

steps.reason: impulse = change in momentum; rebound reverses sign
steps.predictPrompt: Which way does the ball's velocity change sign? Check before subtracting.

steps.result: I = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0 N·s, directed away from the wall
steps.predictPrompt: Would the impulse differ if the ball rebounded at only 10 m/s?

content.question: A 0.5 kg ball thrown at 10 m/s hits a wall and rebounds at 6 m/s. Find the impulse.
hints: rebound means the velocity changes sign — u = +10, v = −6
magnitude 8 N·s; direction away from the wall

content.heading: A harder worked example: the embedded bullet
content.problem: A 0.02 kg bullet travelling at 300 m/s is fired into a wooden block of mass 2 kg resting on a frictionless surface. The bullet embeds itself. Find the velocity of the block immediately after impact.

steps.predictPrompt: Is the block moving before the bullet strikes?

steps.reason: bullet embedded: block and bullet move as one mass
steps.predictPrompt: Do the masses merge in a sticky collision?

steps.result: V = 6 ÷ 2.02 ≈ 2.97 m/s in the bullet's direction
steps.predictPrompt: Why is the answer much smaller than 300 m/s?

content.heading: Go deeper: impulse in crashes, cushions and sport
paragraphs: The tennis follow-through and the cricket soft-catch tell the same physics: extend Δt, and a given Δp needs less force. A ball moving at 20 m/s is caught in 0.05 s or in 0.01 s: for 0.2 kg, Δp = 4 kg·m/s; force = Δp/Δt = 80 N in the soft catch, 400 N in the quick one. Airbags, cushions, bending knees — all of these extend Δt to shrink F.

Sports equipment is designed around impulse. A cricket bat is hit, not pressed — contact Δt is hundredths of a second, which concentrates force at the sweet spot. Contact Δt is a feature of the ball-and-bat combination; the same Δp with a longer Δt softens the peak force without changing the total momentum transferred.

A trampoline and a pillow do not deliver less momentum; they deliver the same momentum over a longer Δt — the total momentum exchanged is identical to the rigid case; only the peak force differs. The safest head rests in a helmet: the shell extends your head's Δt by crushing before the skull does.
bullets: F Δt = Δp — double the time, halve the force
Airbags, helmets, knees bending: longer Δt, smaller F
Same momentum delivered in both cases — only the peak differs
content.takeaway: Impulse protects whatever extends the contact time.

content.heading: Go deeper: reading the force–time graph
paragraphs: Typical JAMB graph questions: the force rises linearly from 0 to a peak (straight-line ramp) and collapses back to 0 — a symmetric triangle. Area = ½ b × h. Another variant shows a force F₁ rising then an opposing constant force F₂ — shaded area above versus below the axis: take the positive area minus the negative.

The staircase graph: force steps at 2 N, 4 N, 6 N for sequential 1 s intervals — momentum change = Σ of rectangle areas = sum, not product. A pulse of 10 N lasting 0.1 s gives 1 N·s — small numbers, but the impulse is not small in a hammer blow.

Trick variants: the y-axis is labelled in N, x-axis in ms — multiply 10⁻³ into the area; the question asks 'momentum change' — that is exactly impulse in disguise. Or it asks for 'velocity after' — divide Δp by the mass first; JAMB never needs a second physical principle past Ft = Δp for these.
bullets: Symmetric ramp up/down → triangle; off-centre → trapezium
Do negatives? subtract areas above/below the axis
Watch the units on the x-axis: ms must become s
content.takeaway: Sweep the graph; area = impulse = Δp.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets questions on collisions
paragraphs: Archetype one: two trolley cars stick together — straightforward mass-weight, one line. Archetype two: the gun recoil — total momentum zero before, ±v after; the gun's recoil speed = mv ÷ M where m is bullet, M is gun (mass ratio always a trick — gun heavier by factor 100, recoil 100 times slower). Archetype three: 'a person of mass X jumps from a boat' — boat shoots away opposite; sign it carefully.

'Which is conserved?' stems ask for momentum versus kinetic energy. Answer momentum; KE only in elastic collisions — JAMB lists this distinction deliberately. 'How much energy is lost?' answers a subtraction of initial minus final KE, not a restitution reflex.

The relative-velocity bridge wins the long problems: before impact the relative speed of approach is u₁ − u₂; the relative speed of separation is v₁ − v₂ — the two are related to elastic bands and elastic 'coefficient 1' case the syllabus skips; but two bodies attracting-then-separating reciprocally is simple addition on a signed axis count. Track signs carefully: velocities in the opposite direction carry opposite signs; momentum survives the signs honestly.
bullets: Gun recoil: v_gun = m v / M — one-line momentum
Conserved: momentum, not KE. KE survives only in elastic hits
Sign with rigour: opposite directions → opposite signs
content.takeaway: Before = after, in momentum; expect one-line arithmetic in JAMB.

lessons.title: Linear Motion and the Equations of Motion
lessons.objective: Interpret distance–time, displacement–time and velocity–time graphs; use v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, s = ½(u + v)t to solve motion problems, including motion under gravity and instantaneous motion.

content.heading: Linear Motion and the Equations of Motion
paragraphs: A Lagos bus pulls away from a junction; its speed rises every second. That rising is acceleration — and its graph is the arithmetic the exam wants.

content.heading: Speed, velocity, acceleration
paragraphs: Speed is distance covered per unit time — a scalar, in m/s. Velocity is displacement per unit time — a vector. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity — a vector: a = (v − u) ÷ t, in m/s².

Average vs instantaneous: the average velocity over a journey is total displacement ÷ total time; the instantaneous velocity at a moment is the gradient of a tangent to the displacement–time curve at that point. JAMB treats 'tangent to a curve' as its standard instantaneous-velocity step.
Uniform acceleration is constant — the net force is constant. If a question mentions changing acceleration, reaching the graph first is safer than reaching for suvat.
bullets: speed = d ÷ t · velocity = Δx ÷ Δt · accel = Δv ÷ Δt
instantaneous = tangent gradient on x–t/s–t curve
suvat: only when acceleration is constant
content.takeaway: Speed, velocity, acceleration — read the slope first, decide later.

check.question: The slope of a velocity–time graph gives the
check.why: Slope = change in velocity ÷ change in time = acceleration.

content.heading: The equations of uniformly accelerated motion
paragraphs: Four equations cover everything: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as; s = ½(u + v)t. Derivation by the v–t line: gradient gives a; the trapezium gives s; substitute v = u + at and all four fall out.
Three of {u, v, a, s, t} known picks the equation with exactly one unknown. Units must match: m, m/s and m/s².
Time law: 'at what instant?' implies v = u + at. Displacement missing: v² = u² + 2as. Time missing: s = ½(u+v)t. Write what you know in a box; circle what you need.
bullets: v = u + at (no displacement) · s = ut + ½at² (no final velocity)
v² = u² + 2as (no time) · s = ½(u + v)t (no acceleration)
Three knowns ⇒ one missing ⇒ exactly one usable equation
content.takeaway: Box the knowns; the equation selects itself.

check.question: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s². The distance covered in 5 s is

content.heading: Motion under gravity and graphs
paragraphs: A falling body is a special uniformly accelerated body — a = g (≈ 9.8 or 10 m/s²), always downward. A stone thrown upward decelerates at g until v = 0 at the top, then accelerates back.
Dropped body: v = gt, s = ½gt², time to fall height h: t = √(2h/g). Upward throw at speed u: max height H = u²/2g, time to top t = u/g, time of flight T = 2u/g (back to launch level).

A distance–time graph with rising slope means increasing speed; a curve bending upward means the body accelerates; a curve flattening means it decelerates. Area under the v–t graph = distance covered — always.
bullets: g = 9.8 m/s² (or 10 in rough problems) — always downward
Top of the throw: v = 0, but acceleration = g downward
d–t curve concave ⇒ accelerating; convex ⇒ decelerating
content.takeaway: Gravity is JAMB's favourite acceleration — u is rarely zero.

check.question: A stone is thrown vertically upward. At the highest point, its velocity is
check.why: Kinetic energy has all become potential — the instantaneous speed is zero, though the acceleration below is still g downward.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Pick one positive direction before you touch a formula — up or forward. g is +9.8 when down is positive, −9.8 otherwise; every sign in suvat depends on the same choice.

content.problem: A car accelerates uniformly from 15 m/s to 35 m/s in 5 s. Find (a) the acceleration, (b) the distance covered in those 5 s.

steps.predictPrompt: Which suvat equation holds when time is known but distance is not?
Between two speeds, is average speed the safe route here?

content.question: A body dropped from rest falls freely. Find (a) its velocity after 3 s, (b) the distance covered in the first 3 s. Take g = 10 m/s².

content.heading: A harder worked example: up and down
content.problem: A stone is thrown upward at 20 m/s. Find (a) max height, (b) time to top, (c) total flight time. Take g = 10 m/s².

steps.reason: at the top v = 0; v² = u² − 2gH
steps.predictPrompt: Which v do you substitute at the top of the throw?

steps.reason: v = u − gt; v = 0 → t = u ÷ g
steps.predictPrompt: Does the stone stop accelerating at the top for an instant, or does g keep working?
If the stone is caught at a lower point, will T be bigger or smaller?

content.heading: Go deeper: deriving the equations from graphs
paragraphs: Take the v–t graph of a uniformly accelerated body: a straight line from (0, u) to (t, v). The gradient of the line is (v − u) ÷ t, and that is definitionally the acceleration a. Rearranged: v = u + at.

The area under the line is a trapezium — ½ (u + v) × t — and the area in a velocity–time graph is displacement, so s = ½(u + v)t. Substitute v = u + at: s = ½(u + u + at)t = ut + ½at². Eliminate t instead of s: v² = u² + 2as.

Every one of the four equations is just bookkeeping on the same straight line. JAMB will not ask you to prove them in the exam; it will ask you to pick the right one. The four-known-data rule keeps the choice honest: with u, v, a, s, t in play, three knowns pick the equation with exactly one unknown.
bullets: v-t line → gradient = a, area = s
Know 3 of {u, v, a, s, t} → the equation writes itself
Eliminate the missing variable, not the hard one
content.takeaway: Graphs are the engine; equations are the gearbox.

content.heading: Go deeper: gravity in both directions
paragraphs: Upward: u positive; stone leaving the hand at 20 m/s, rock decelerating at 10 m/s each second — 10 m/s at 1 s, 0 at 2 s. The 'stopping' is velocity only; acceleration never ceases and never changes sign. At the top, kinetic energy equals zero and potential energy peaks; total energy is unchanged ignoring drag.

Downward: freely falling or released, u ≥ 0; velocity grows by 10 m/s every second — 10, 20, 30 — and distance fallen compounds as 5, 15, 30, 45 m in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th seconds. Because s ∝ t², each successive second adds more distance than the last.

Escape-direction rule: a stone thrown upward released at 35 m/s and another released from rest that has fallen freely for 1 s both have speed 35−10*0=35 vs 10 — a symmetric place on the same parabola of motion, just opposite directions. Trajectories in one dimension never cross themselves; velocity sign flips, path does not.
bullets: at the top: v = 0; a = g always (there is no zero-acceleration instant)
distance each second grows: 5, 15, 25, 35 m drops in 1..4 s
up-flight time = down-flight time back to the same level
content.takeaway: Gravity never rests — not even at the peak.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets graph and suvat questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) read off u, v and t from a tabulated graph and compute a = Δv/Δt; (2) shade the area on the v–t graph and compute distance; (3) given two moments, decide whether the body accelerates or decelerates from the gradient; (4) trap stems say 'falls freely' — u = 0, a = g, always; (5) 'thrown vertically downward at 20 m/s' — u = 20, a = g, still downward; (6) 'reaches the point in 2 s but is caught 2 m downwind of release' — horizontal datum misleading — read signs, not the story.

Curved d–t graphs: 'instantaneous velocity' asks for the gradient of the tangent at that point — draw it, read two clear points off it. A d–t parabola indicates uniformly increasing speed — a = constant, v growing linearly. The inverse: v grows linearly ⇒ d grows as t².

Rare exceptions JAMB tolerates: motion through a hole or cliff — 'dropped from rest' then 'hits the water'; chain two phases — free-fall then decelerate? No — a body under gravity cannot decelerate on its own unless air pushes back; any mention of 'constant velocity fall' implies terminal velocity and not JAMB-level revision of this topic — but the questions about air resistance flag it as 'not JAMB material' — skip it.
bullets: 'Falls freely' = u 0 + a g=10. 'Vertically downward at u' = u>0 + a g
instantaneous velocity = tangent gradient, two far points on it
linear v ⇒ quadratic x; curved x ⇒ non-constant v
content.takeaway: The graph is the arithmetic — learn the readout before the formula.

lessons.title: Projectile Motion
lessons.objective: Separate horizontal and vertical motion, derive expressions for range, maximum height and time of flight from the ground and from a height; solve worked projectile problems including rocket and missile applications.

content.heading: Projectile Motion
paragraphs: A striker chips the ball and it arcs into the net. Two motions live in that arc — a steady sideways glide, and the same rise-and-fall as a stone thrown up.

content.heading: Splitting the motion into two axes
paragraphs: A launched projectile splits into horizontal motion (no force, no acceleration — velocity u cos θ, constant through the whole flight) and vertical motion (constant acceleration, g acting downward).
u cos θ = uₓ, u sin θ = u_y. At all times: x = u cos θ · t, y = u sin θ · t − ½gt². The curve, when time is eliminated, is a parabola.
Upward or downward launched — the same split holds. The sign of u_y depends on the angle above or below the horizontal; r_components always come in this pair.
bullets: horizontal: aₓ = 0, uₓ = u cos θ constant
vertical: a_y = g (down), u_y = u sin θ
x = uₓt · y = u_y t − ½gt² — the parabola itself
content.takeaway: Horizontal keeps; vertical performs — never the same account.

check.question: In projectile motion, ignoring air resistance, the horizontal velocity of the projectile is
check.why: No horizontal force acts, so horizontal velocity never changes.

content.heading: Range, maximum height and time of flight
paragraphs: Up and down motion takes the same time both ways. Time to peak t = u sin θ ÷ g; total time of flight T = 2u sin θ ÷ g.
Maximum height H = u² sin² θ ÷ 2g. Hold that, or derive from v² = u² − 2gH at the peak.
Range from launch to landing at the same level: R = u² sin 2θ ÷ g. Its biggest value occurs at 45°, where sin 90° = 1. R at θ and at (90° − θ) are equal in range — e.g., 30° and 60°.
bullets: T = 2usinθ ÷ g · H = u²sin²θ ÷ 2g · R = u²sin2θ ÷ g
Largest range at 45°
θ = 30° and θ = 60° fly the same distance
content.takeaway: T, H and R are all one memorised trio — the same vertical motion, rotated three ways.

content.heading: From a height above the ground
paragraphs: From a cliff, y drops to the foot — replace the landing level with −h. The fall time becomes √(2h ÷ g) (ascent time adds only at steep angles).
Horizontal launch from height h: t = √(2h ÷ g); range = u × √(2h ÷ g). No u component of u_y exists, so the object is simply in free fall for u × t metres sideways.
Applications: missiles after fuel cutoff, football throw-ins, discus and shot put — launched high on purpose for a longer fall and further flight.
bullets: horizontal launch: t = √(2h ÷ g), R = u × t
the equation changes, not the physics — only the Δy
lift off high ⇒ longer fall time ⇒ further range
content.takeaway: The formula book is identical; only the final Δy is different.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Horizontal and vertical motions are strangers to each other; only the clock is shared. Do the two problems separately, then add what is asked.

content.problem: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find (a) the time of flight, (b) the maximum height, (c) the range. Take g = 10 m/s².

content.heading: Go deeper: the projectile in one master sketch
paragraphs: Draw the launch velocity and split it. Horizontal side is a flat line — the projectile's x-axis, unchanged all flight. Vertical side rises, peaks at u_y = 0, and descends. Mirror image on both sides of the peak — the time up equals the time down if the launch and landing levels are the same.

Eliminating t between the two: y = x tan θ − (g ÷ 2u² cos² θ) x². That is the equation of the trajectory — a quadratic; at y = 0 one recovers the range; at the vertex one recovers the maximum height. JAMB rarely demands you recite it but understanding it pays off when 'angle for maximum range' appears.

45 degrees: sin 2θ max at θ = 45°; ranges from any of the 30°/60° pairs come out identical; range at 80° is far shorter — sin 160° = sin 20° small — which is why highlob lobbing rarely wins matches except in desperate situations.
bullets: throw split → flat horizontal line + symmetric arc
y = x tanθ − (g ÷ 2u² cos²θ) x² is the trajectory
45° wins the range; 30° and 60° share it
content.takeaway: The parabola is the same shape whether launched at 45°, 60° or 80°.

content.heading: Go deeper: launches from above the ground
paragraphs: Set the ground as y = 0; the launch point is now at y = h. Vertical equation: h = u_y t − ½gt² with opposite signs for downward launches; solve the quadratic and pick the positive root. For shallow angles the ascending half barely registers, and the whole flight is essentially a delayed fall.

Best mental shortcut: horizontal launch with speed u from height h — fall time t = √(2h/g), independent of u. That independence is a classic JAMB probe: 'a stone dropped and a stone projected horizontally land at the same instant' — both fall the same height, so both arrive together.

For angled launches from a height, drop-height + up-travel stack — the peak comes higher than the launch, and the extra fall distance is (h + H). Applys the same v² = u² − 2as; ranges grow. The sign of u_y makes the only difference from the flat-ground case. If the launch is below the level — a hole or dockside shot — total fall distance is (h − H_if_ascending_finishes_above_zero…) — subtract; don't chase the angle for small h.
bullets: horizontal launch: t = √(2h ÷ g) irrespective of u
from above ground: stack H onto h, then y = h + … → solve
dropped and horizontally projected hit together — same fall h
content.takeaway: Height changes the numbers, never the bookkeeping.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets projectile questions
paragraphs: The archetypes: (1) given u, θ: find T, H or R, or the reverse; (2) 'the same range at 30°' — deduce sin 60°; (3) 'angle for maximum range' — 45°; (4) 'the horizontal and vertical components at impact' — horizontal stays u cos θ; vertical = u sin θ − gT; (5) 'the resultant velocity at impact' — square root of the squares of the two; (6) 'at what instant does the projectile have zero vertical velocity' — t = u sin θ ÷ g, always, no trick.

Rocket flight: powered rocket phase is not projectile motion — thrust dominates; the phase after fuel runs out matches it exactly. Missiles and projectiles: same as the ballistic arc after cutoff. A 'missile fired at 60°' exam stem asks exactly the u, θ, T, H, R block — not thrust calculations; rockets are a story dressing, not a new physics model.

Common wrong answer JAMB plants: 'the horizontal velocity at the highest point is zero.' NO — the projectile never loses horizontal velocity; only the vertical stops. The second plant: 'the acceleration differs between the up phase and the down phase' — no: g is one sign, never reversed. The third plant: 'the speed at impact is less than the speed at launch' — no: at the same level, energy conservation mikes the two speeds identical (neglecting air resistance).
bullets: horizontal at the peak: NOT zero · g: same up and down
impacts at the same level: launch speed = impact speed
rockets: thrust phase — not projectile; fuel out = projectile
content.takeaway: The whole topic is one diagram with three formulas.

lessons.title: Circular Motion
lessons.objective: Use radians, angular velocity and angular acceleration; apply centripetal force F = mv²/r = mω²r; distinguish centripetal from centrifugal force and solve circular-motion problems in strings, satellite orbits and bends.

content.heading: Circular Motion
paragraphs: A car whips round a corner; the passengers lean outward. A long stone on a string loops round overhead. Both are the same mathematics — the mathematics of angular motion, where every second the body turns through an angle rather than stepping forward.

content.heading: Angular displacement and angular speed
paragraphs: Angles in radians: a complete circle is 2π radians. An arc length s subtending at the centre: s = rθ. For circular motion, θ (radians) = angle turned, measured from a reference radius.

Angular velocity ω (omega) is the rate of turning: ω = θ ÷ t. One complete revolution in T seconds ⇒ ω = 2π ÷ T = 2πf. Its unit is the radian per second (rad/s). Angular acceleration α is the rate of change of ω: α = Δω ÷ Δt (rad/s²).
bullets: 1 revolution = 2π rad; rad is dimensionless, label it anyway
ω = θ ÷ t = 2πf = 2π ÷ T (rad/s)
linear and angular link: v = rω, a = rα
content.takeaway: Think in revolutions first; multiply by 2π only in the last line.

check.question: A wheel makes 60 revolutions per minute. Its angular speed in rad/s is
check.why: 60 rev/min = 1 rev/s = 2π rad each second.

content.heading: Centripetal force
paragraphs: Anything in uniform circular motion is accelerating toward the centre — acceleration a = v² ÷ r = ω²r, always pointed inward along the radius. The force supplying it is the centripetal force: F = mv² ÷ r = mω²r.

Friction supplies it on a dry bend; tension on a string rides a stone overhead; gravity keeps a satellite gripped to its orbit. Remove the inward force and the body flies off along a tangent — exactly the way a stone leaves the string when the string snaps.
bullets: F = mv² ÷ r = mω²r — toward the centre, never outward
providers: friction, tension, gravity, spring, magnetic
String snaps ⇒ object departs along a tangent, not radially
content.takeaway: Inward force or the body leaves along a tangent — radius guides its run.

check.question: A 1000 kg car moves at 10 m/s on a level curve of radius 50 m. The centripetal force on it is

content.heading: Centripetal versus centrifugal — and applications
paragraphs: Centripetal force is real: the inward pull. Centrifugal force is the 'outward' pull you feel inside a rotating frame — a pseudo-force that only recipes inside a body sharing that frame's rotation; balance is still provided by the real friction or tension.

Applications: a satellite holds an orbit because gravity acts as its centripetal force; a car slides on a wet bend when friction alone cannot supply the required inward force; washing machine spinners use the small leftover outward way to fling water through holes; centrifuges — blood, milk, air — speed up separation.
JAMB loves magnitude comparison: a heavier body needs a proportionally bigger inward force at the same speed and radius; a longer radius at the same speed needs a smaller inward force.
bullets: centrifugal is the apparent outward force inside rotating frames
all satellites: gravity = centripetal force
F ∝ m, F ∝ v², F ∝ 1/r — measure direction always inward
content.takeaway: Centripetal is the real keeper; centrifugal is the echo inside the spinning car.

check.question: An object in uniform circular motion has a velocity that is directed
options: perpendicular to the radius, along the tangent
check.why: Velocity is along the tangent; it is acceleration and force that point toward the centre.

content.heading: Go deeper: radians and revolutions
paragraphs: Radians save calculator keystrokes. One full turn is 2π radians; half a turn is π; a right angle is π ÷ 2. A wheel turning at 10 rad/s covers an arc of 10 × r units every second; for a point 0.5 m out, that is 5 m/s at the rim.

Angular acceleration ramps the speed of angular turn: α = Δω ÷ Δt. JAMB pairs α with the statement 'angular velocity is now ω'. Given starting ω, time, and final ω, α follows in one line. Angular displacement also matters: θ = initial ω · t + ½αt² — the rotational cousin of s = ut + ½at².

Connecting rotation to linear motion: every point on the body shares the same ω; the linear speed is greater the further out you sit — v = rω. JAMB loves the question comparing the rim and the hub of the same wheel — different linear v, identical ω at both locations.
bullets: v = rω — same ω for whole wheel, v varies with r
rotational suvat mirror: θ = ω₀t + ½αt²
content.takeaway: Radians are just a rotated ruler — they carry all the same equations.

content.heading: Go deeper: where the inward force comes from
paragraphs: A satellite holds orbit in free fall: gravity points at Earth, but the tangential velocity is so large that the stone continually misses — the orbit is the result of 'falling forever toward Earth yet always missing' — the textbook line for satellites (Newton's mountain thought experiment).

A car on a flat bend relies on friction between tyre and tarmac as its inward provider: F = mv² ÷ r ≤ μN; above that speed the car slides outward — not because of a new force outward, but because friction is simply no longer enough; the car's inertia keeps it straight.

Washing machine spin cycle: the drum acts as a rotating frame — inside it, water gets flung to the drum wall while the drum drills holes allowing it out; your clothes stay in the drum afterwards because the friction between cloth and drum holds them in. Centrifuges separate blood — cells pushed to the end by inertia in the rotating frame.
bullets: gravity = centripetal force in every free-fall orbit
μmg ≥ mv²/r for grip — exceed it and the car slides straight on
centrifuges: rotation sends heavier components outward first
content.takeaway: Centripetal providers are ordinary forces doing an extraordinary job.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets circular-motion questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'from n revolutions per minute, find ω in rad/s' — divide by 60, multiply by 2π; (2) 'a satellite orbits in T minutes — find its speed given the radius' — v = 2πr/T; (3) 'the tension on the string' — T = mv²/r; (4) 'the angular acceleration' — gradient of ω–t line or α = Δω/t; (5) 'at what speed does the car skid' — μgr under the square root for v_max.

Trap stems: 'centrifugal force is larger on the equator' — no; the inward providers supply exactly mv²/r; centrifugal is pseudo; JAMB tests the inertia language and the missing-friction idea instead. Another trap: 'the unit of centripetal force is N directed outward' — outward is never an answer; inward is default.

Ordering: radius, period, mass come in any combination; convert hours to seconds, minutes to seconds; never answer in rad/min — JAMB expects rad/s. In satellite problems, the formula cycles turn often: v = 2πr/T then F = mv²/r — two steps both expected; the last wraps up the force.
bullets: f → ω: v = 2πfr — always convert at the first line
outward force is never the answer — centripetal is inward
v_max for grip = √(μgr)
content.takeaway: Circular motion is three formulas in a trench coat — learn three, pass most stems.

lessons.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
lessons.objective: Define simple harmonic motion, identify oscillators, use T = 1/f, T = 2π√(l/g) and T = 2π√(m/k); compute v and a from ω; analyse energy changes; identify forced vibrations and resonance with applications.

content.heading: Simple Harmonic Motion
paragraphs: Watch a pendulum swing; pluck a guitar string; press a tuning fork — all keep time with the same mathematics: simple harmonic motion.

content.heading: What simple harmonic motion is
paragraphs: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is a motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and directed toward that point — a = −ω²x.

The fixed point is the mean position. The displacement from it swings between extremes (amplitudes). Every oscillator with equal opportunity on both sides of the mean — pendulum, tuning fork, spring-mass system, plucked string — obeys SHM when one keeps angle small.
Amplitude A is the maximum displacement. Period T is the time of one full back-and-forth; frequency f = 1 ÷ T. JAMB also uses the term 'oscillatory motion' — SHM is its quantitative case.
bullets: definition: a = −ω²x — acceleration → mean, proportional to x
examples: pendulum, tuning fork, spring-mass, vibrating string
A = max displacement; T = seconds per cycle; f = 1 ÷ T
content.takeaway: The minus sign is the whole story — acceleration always pulls back to the mean.

check.question: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration of the body is directed
check.why: a = −ω²x — the minus sign forces acceleration to point opposite to displacement, i.e., toward the mean position.

content.heading: Period, frequency and the two formulas
paragraphs: f × T = 1; f = 1 ÷ T and T = 1 ÷ f. The angular frequency ω = 2π ÷ T = 2πf. Velocity: v = ω√(A² − x²); maximum v at the mean position: v_max = ωA. Acceleration: a = −ω²x; maximum at extremes: a_max = ω²A.
Pendulum: T = 2π√(l ÷ g). Doubling length quadruples T in squared time — no, doubles √l by √2 times, actually multiplies T by √2. Under small angle only.
Spring: T = 2π√(m ÷ k). Stiffer spring (larger k) ⇒ shorter T; more mass ⇒ longer T. Mass does not affect the pendulum's period at all (small-angle approximation); it does affect the spring's.
bullets: pendulum: T = 2π√(l ÷ g)
spring: T = 2π√(m ÷ k)
content.takeaway: Escape by formula: square root ratios of (l/g) or (m/k) decide T.

check.question: A simple pendulum of length 1 m swings at a place where g = 10 m/s². Its period is about

content.heading: Energy, forced vibrations and resonance
paragraphs: As a body swings through SHM, its total energy stays constant (no friction): T.E. = ½mω²A². Kinetic energy peaks at the mean position; potential energy peaks at the extremes. Both move from one side to the other; sum is fixed.
Equations: K.E. = ½mω²(A² − x²); P.E. = ½mω²x²; total = ½mω²A². JAMB's favourite wording: 'the ratio of KE to PE at general x or given instant' — plug equations and simplify.
Forced vibration: an object driven by an external periodic force, oscillating at the driver’s frequency. Resonance: driving frequency = natural frequency — amplitude peaks to maximum.
bullets: total energy constant; mix of KE and PE at every instant
K.E. max at mean; P.E. max at extremes
resonance: driver frequency = natural frequency ⇒ amplitude peaks
content.takeaway: KE buys amplitude at the mean; PE saves it at the extremes.

check.question: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency
options: is lower than the natural frequency
is higher than the natural frequency
check.why: Energy transfers most efficiently at matching frequencies — the definition of resonance.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: v, a and T questions rarely leave SHM: the three must-know symbols are ω, A, x. Keep the three symbols on your desk from the start of the question.

content.heading: Go deeper: deriving the pendulum and spring periods
paragraphs: A pendulum of length l displaced by small angle θ swings because of the restoring component mg sin θ ≈ mg θ. Newton's second law along the arc: ml²(θ'' ) = −mgl θ → θ'' = −(g ÷ l) θ. Comparing a = −ω²x gives ω² = g ÷ l, so T = 2π√(l ÷ g). The algebra requires the small-angle trick — sin θ ≈ θ — JAMB never asks you to prove this but knowing it sharpens the formula's meaning.

Check this from the energy side: K.E. + P.E. cancelling out gives total = ½m g × x_height rise = a spiral decay without damping. For a spring: F = −kx, m(a) = −kx with x'' = −(k ÷ m) x, so ω² = k ÷ m, so T = 2π√(m ÷ k).

There is no mass in the pendulum formula — increasing mass raises both inertia and gravitational pull equally; they cancel. JAMB loves exactly this twist: 'what happens to T if mass increases' — no change, provided l, and g, are unchanged.
bullets: small angle: sin θ ≈ θ enables everything
ω² pendulum = g ÷ l; ω² spring = k ÷ m
mass cancels out of the pendulum period — independent
content.takeaway: Periods come from the restoring force constant — not the mass alone.

content.heading: Go deeper: energy through a full swing
paragraphs: At the mean position: x = 0, so P.E. = 0 and v = v_max — K.E. = ½ m ω² A² = the full total energy. At the extreme: v = 0, so K.E. = 0 and P.E. = ½ m ω² A² = total. At general x: K.E. = ½ m ω² (A² − x²), P.E. = ½ m ω² x². The pair sums to ½ m ω² A² at every x — the invariant.

For a spring: total energy = ½ k A². JAMB may mix: 'behold, a spring of stiffness 400 N/m stretched 0.1 m — how much energy stored?' answer into P.E. against the spring: ½ × 400 × 0.01 = 2 J. When set free, the mass moves through with KE peaks 2 J as it crosses the mean.

Real systems decay: friction and drag bleed energy — amplitude falls over time (damping). Underdamped systems oscillate smaller and smaller; critical damping stops the motion in the shortest time — shock absorbers; overdamping drags slowly — doors on museums, brakes to the floor.
bullets: mean: KE max · PE zero · extremes reverse
½ m ω² A² (mass-spring)· ½ k A² (spring energy)
damping: energy loss till stop · critical: fastest · overdamped: slow
content.takeaway: Total energy is the only fixed book in the library — both ledgers dance in step.

content.heading: Go deeper: forced vibrations and resonance
paragraphs: Natural (free) frequency: an object oscillating freely after a single kick at its own rate. Forced frequency: an object driven by external rhythm; the object swings at the driving frequency, not at its own. Every building, bridge, machine and molecule prefers one rate; force it off that rate and it resists; force it at that rate and amplitudes climb dangerously.

Resonance test cases: soldiers route-march on a bridge — the bridge may start swaying at its own natural rate to the boot rhythm; soldiers break step crossing. Radio antenna: the incoming radio wave carries one EM frequency; antenna resonates only at the station's; tunes away the others off — strong reception.

Shadow applications: microwave ovens resonate the water molecule 2.45 GHz — food heats. A singer at a soda-go glass's natural frequency cracks the glass. Drums and piano chords — the string lifting its amplitude when the resonator box matches — acoustics exploits resonance deliberately. Negative roles: machinery hum ramps into fatigue, phone vibration builds at cover frequencies; insurance note counts these.
bullets: free frequency = the object's own; forced = the driver's
matching rates = resonance = max amplitude
examples: bridges, radios, microwaves, glass breaking — soldiers break step
content.takeaway: Forced is a car listening to the road; resonance is the bridge deciding to agree.
